1:
The sword comes first, described three times over. Gill offers a choice: the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, or some judgment in history, found by some in the Medes and Persians breaking the Babylonian monarchy; he settles on the power of God itself, the two-edged sword out of the mouth of the Word, slaying the antichristian kings. Henry hears the emphasis in the original and will not let translation flatten it: the Lord with his sword, that cruel one, that great one, that strong one. The stroke is not a keeper's dispatch of a dangerous animal, he says, but a traitor's execution, the wages of this creature's sin being death. Ellicott makes the three epithets structural, sore and swift and strong, and guesses the sword began as the lightning-flash before it became a figure of judgment.

Clarke, following Lowth, begins with zoology. The three names are three creatures: the crocodile, so rigid along the backbone that he cannot easily turn while pursuing prey, whom one escapes by short frequent turnings; the dragon, flexible and winding, coiling into a circle; and the sea monster or whale. That they stand allegorically for great potentates he does not doubt; which potentates is another matter, and he declines it as a difficulty his notes need not settle. He passes on Kimchi's answer instead: leviathan is a parable concerning the kings of the Gentiles, the three names carrying the Grecian, Turkish and Roman empires, the sea-dragon a nation of strong navy and wide commerce.

Ellicott answers what Clarke refused. Three epithets mean three empires, drawn as monstrous animal forms after the manner of the later visions. The dragon is Egypt, its standing emblem elsewhere. The other two are so alike in kind that one word serves both, each marked off by its adjective, and he assigns them to Assyria and Babylon; the adjectives answer to their rivers, the rush of the Tigris against the windings of the Euphrates, and beyond the rivers to the policy of each state, one aggressive by open speed, the other advancing by sinuous deceit. He reports the rivals fairly: some read Egypt in all three clauses, and Cheyne finds no earthly empire, but rebel powers of evil and darkness.

Calvin takes that last road furthest. He has no doubt the verse speaks allegorically of Satan's whole kingdom, described as a monstrous animal, with a glance at the wiles that gloss over his designs; and though it fits the king of Egypt, that one class was meant to hold every other enemy of the church. Then he corrects himself: the passage concerns not Satan personally but the agents by which he governs. His application is nautical: we have continually to do with him as with a wild beast, and the world is the sea we sail, where such beasts work to upset the ship, and we have no defence unless the Lord aids us. He is permitted for a time to fortify his kingdom, but the war is not over, and an enemy vanquished a hundred times keeps renewing it.

The rest is naming enemies. Henry finds the church troubled by many and usually by one worse than the rest, Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus each in his day, Pharaoh before them all; the newer church has its own, a great red dragon ready to devour. He distributes the images: leviathan for bulk and strength and the bustle such powers make, dragon for rage, piercing serpent for penetrating counsel and quick motion, a creature that having got its head in draws its whole body after, crooked serpent for what is subtle and insinuating. Wesley refuses the distribution and makes all three names one thing, a powerful enemy whose sting goes deep and whose winding shows craft, its strength making the craft more formidable. Both end where Gill did, at a stronger arm broken.
2:
The song is antiphonal, or it is no song at all. Clarke, following Lowth, renders the opening sing ye a responsive song, the verb bearing that sense, and sets the parts out like a score, Jehovah speaking, then the vineyard, then Jehovah again. He calls this the ancient method in many nations, a dialogue in verse delivered much as recitative is now, instancing the song of Deborah, Theocritus and Virgil. Ellicott needs no dialogue: the prophet reappears as hymn writer of the coming day, having chanted a dirge over an unfruitful vineyard and now turning wailing into poem. Gill takes the singing as the church's alternating response, but reports Gussetius reading the imperative the other way round, afflict her, a dare flung at the enemies.

The wine is disputed in the same breath. Clarke passes on Kimchi's rule that the redder the wine the higher its value; Wesley agrees, the choicest wine in those parts being red. Calvin generalises: red stands in Scripture for excellence, and the vineyard's worth comes from its soil and cultivation, which is to say from undeserved favour continued without a break. Ellicott renders the word fiery or foaming. Lowth abandons the colour, reading a beloved vineyard on the authority of the Septuagint and Chaldee, and Ellicott grants the Greek looks to have had another text before it, one letter apart.

Then the keeper speaks. Gill puts the weight on the first person: unless he keeps it the watchmen wake in vain, and he keeps it from the reign of sin, Satan's temptations, the world's malice, the poison of false teachers and any final falling away. Ellicott reads a reversal of the older vineyard song, clause answering clause: for abandonment, constant care; for clouds ordered to withhold rain, watering whenever wanted; for the wild boar let in, a guard day and night. Calvin names the two things a vineyard needs, cultivation and protection, and supplies the interval the promise passes over, when God seemed to have laid care aside and the vineyard differed little from a wilderness. Clarke finds manuscripts making even the visiting God's own act.

The fourth verse divides them most sharply. Ellicott, Gill, Calvin and Wesley hear God disclaiming wrath. Gill grounds it in substitution, the wrath his people deserved being borne by another. Calvin makes it a father who pities while offended, whose love outruns his anger and who is perverse only towards the perverse; he then hears God complain that he would sooner fight briers than his own inheritance, and dismisses as too forced for refutation the reading that has God working himself into a rage. Clarke will have none of it. With Lowth he reads a wall for the wrath, one letter apart, giving the line to the vineyard: I have no wall. He weighs his evidence honestly, admitting no manuscript supports the change and the Greek settles nothing, and rests the case on the older song, where the wall was the thing taken away.

The close is growth. Gill reads the coming ones as Jacob's own seed, Israelites indeed, rooted and grounded, though he allows the other construction, those who come to Jacob. Ellicott renders it future, Jacob striking root, and lets the psalm of the church end there. Delitzsch marks where figure gives way and prophecy resumes, the prophet saying what the apostle would later say of that root; his note on the serpents runs to the Euphrates, cut about so artificially that a traveller in Herodotus passed one village thrice in three days. Calvin hears a promise to a diminished church: reduced to a very small number, it will still fill the world, for however far wrath cuts us down the roots are not killed but hidden. Henry sets the gospel church deeper and wider. Wesley takes the fruit for colonies abroad, then thinks better and makes the seed spiritual.
7:
The seventh verse is a comparison that can run two ways. Most take it that God has not struck his own as he struck those who struck them. Gill lists the final strokes: the plagues and the Red Sea, the angel in Sennacherib's camp overnight, Amalek whose memory perished, the Babylon still to fall; Israel went captive and came back, is scattered now and still a people. Wesley says it in a line: God has not dealt so severely with his own as with the enemies he utterly destroyed. Delitzsch places the prophet inside the punishment, certain Israel will not be lifted up until deeply humbled, and sees from there that what God inflicts on Israel differs from what he inflicts on the world.

Ellicott lets the other reading stand. He fixes the pronouns, which the English leaves obscure, then reports the version some critics prefer: not that God struck Israel unlike the way he struck her oppressors, but that he did not strike her as they struck her, ruthlessly and in hate, remembering mercy in wrath. Calvin canvasses both, prefers the received, and turns it into a distinction between elect and reprobate. Against the reprobate God gives his anger loose rein, having no object but to destroy; chastising the godly he restrains it, meaning to bring them back. He knows why the sentence goes round about: God commonly uses wicked men as his instrument, and to be handed to their tyranny is a sore temptation, since we cannot tell whether he favours them or abandons us.

The measure is the mercy. Gill hears God contending not only with his people but with the affliction itself, checking it and refusing to let it pass bounds. Calvin makes the moderation a rule without exception: we could not bear God's hand unheld, and he is faithful, as Paul says, not to let us be tried past our strength. He then puts three readings of the shooting forth in order, rejects two, allows the stroke may reach the plants as well as the person, and settles on the root: God cuts down branches and even trunk but never lets the root die, while the reprobate he tears up altogether. Wesley keeps the picture in miniature, the luxuriant branches cut off but the vine spared.

Ellicott will not have the picture. He renders the clause as divorce: when thou didst put her away, thou didst plead with her, falling back on an earlier prophet's adulterous wife, dismissed without pressing the plea to the limit the law allowed. He does the same to the next clause, and Delitzsch is with him. The familiar reading has God staying the rough wind lest a man be swallowed up by too much sorrow; but the word means sifting, not staying, and he sifts with the rough wind in the day of the east wind. Punishment does follow punishment, and is still reformatory rather than penal. Ellicott notes a third possibility: God sighs with his rough wind, a sorrow mixed into the chastisement.

Then the purpose, and a controversy Calvin cannot pass. Gill denies flatly that afflictions atone; they bring a man to see his sin and drive him to a sacrifice not his own. Calvin takes the harder form: if punishment expiates, then where it is absent satisfactions must replace it. He answers that chastisements expiate indirectly and never directly, being remedies that consume our desires as fire does and prepare us for the repentance that obtains pardon. Henry observes that judgment begins at the house of God, and those he has known above all families of the earth he punishes first. Ellicott divides proof from instrument, and finds Josiah breaking altar stones and sun-pillars in a deliberate attempt to fulfil the condition set here. Wesley dates the oracle by an altar of Ahaz still standing; Clarke adds a conjunction from four manuscripts.
10:
Which city is desolate divides them three ways. Delitzsch says Jerusalem, and takes the consequence: the prophet must stand beyond its destruction, in the captivity, watching punishment end where sin ends. Calvin says Jerusalem too, chiefly, though the threat covers all Judea; the godly would lose heart at that city overthrown and the temple pulled down, and this was written to meet the temptation and show God has methods enough to preserve his church. Wesley adds the other fortified towns. Gill will have none of it, naming and refusing Jerusalem, Samaria and literal Babylon alike, and putting in their place mystical Babylon, Rome and the whole antichristian jurisdiction. Ellicott moves the other way on a verbal clue, the same phrase standing earlier for the city of the strangers; the enemy's desolation answers the purified city of the verse before, and Jerusalem here breaks the sequence.

The calves crop the branches, and the branches will not last. Gill makes the city a tree whose boughs, gnawed by cattle, dry in a hot summer till they snap, fit for nothing but burning. Ellicott furnishes the ruin differently, shrubs over the open spaces, perhaps gardens inside walls like Babylon's, where women gather firewood without fear of trespass. Calvin objects: the ambiguous word means harvest as readily as bough, and he takes it so, the grain cut before it ripens, the produce a man thought already in his hand taken out of it. Clarke keeps the vine and explains why wood is gathered at all: fuel is so scarce in the east that dung, roots and fruit parings are burnt, vine twigs particularly, gathered by women and children and laid up in store.

Calvin finds the disgrace in who gathers. God needs no soldiers and uses women, unused to war, which makes the plundering more humiliating than defeat. Wesley reaches it shorter: women are mentioned because the men will be dead. Then the reason, a people of no understanding, on which Calvin builds: ignorance is the source of all evils, the fear of God being where wisdom begins; yet it excuses nobody, for the man blinded by lust still knows what he does, and Hebrew usage lets the one word stand for every kind of sin. Wesley hears the last clause break their confidence that God would never destroy his own handiwork.

Ellicott alone lets it fall elsewhere. The words are generic, he grants, and elsewhere describe Israel as apostate; here context turns the scale towards the world-power, and so taken show the prophet believing the God of Israel made the heathen nations too. The gathering that follows is threshing. Calvin has the people so buried under the captivity that they were grain under chaff, needing a fan to find them, and expects them brought back one after another, as scattered men are. Wesley and Delitzsch keep grain and rod. Ellicott changes the crop: the verb is used of beating down olives, and against the earlier gleaning of a few from the topmost boughs this is a full harvest, each single olive cared for.

The rivers are the old boundaries. Ellicott makes the flood the Euphrates and denies the stream of Egypt is the Nile, naming the wadi dividing Palestine from Egypt, which the Greeks called Rhinocolura. Calvin needs both a Chaldean and an Egyptian exile, some carried to Babylon, many fleeing the other way, and presses that those who fled to Egypt disobeyed a plain command and are gathered anyway. Clarke alone takes the channel for the river Sabbation, on Kimchi's authority. The trumpet closes it. Wesley hears the camp signal, Calvin kings mustering armies, prophecy having no less force; Ellicott traces the figure from the silver trumpets of the wilderness marches and the jubilee to later apocalypses. Clarke turns it on his own century, expecting Egypt to receive the gospel once the Ottoman yoke is thrown off.
